nameStory: Yellow sundrops get their cheerful name from their bright golden flowers that open during the day, unlike many of their evening primrose relatives that bloom at night. The 'sundrops' name perfectly captures how these sunny blooms seem to glow like drops of liquid sunshine in the garden. Some botanists also call this species 'glaucous evening primrose' because of its blue-green waxy leaf coating.
description: Yellow sundrops is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms neat clumps about 1-2 feet tall and wide. It produces bright yellow, four-petaled flowers that bloom during the day from late spring through summer. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive blue-green, waxy coating that gives them a silvery appearance. Despite being in the evening primrose family, this species opens its cheerful blooms in daylight rather than at dusk.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four silky petals arranged in a cross pattern, each bloom about 1-2 inches across with a sweet, delicate fragrance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive blue-green waxy coating that feels smooth and slightly thick to the touch, arranged alternately along reddish stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading clumps that stay compact and tidy, rarely exceeding 2 feet in height with a mounding growth pattern

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops narrow, four-angled seed capsules that split open when ripe to release small seeds with a papery texture

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Often show attractive reddish coloring, especially toward the base, and feel sturdy but not woody when gently squeezed

habitat: Yellow sundrops thrive in sunny, well-drained locations including meadows, prairies, and garden borders throughout New England. They prefer sandy or loamy soils and are often found in areas that get full sun for most of the day. This species is quite adaptable and can handle both slightly dry conditions and occasional moisture.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as blue-green rosettes of leaves, with flower buds beginning to form in late spring as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers opening during the day from June through August, attracting bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, while leaves may develop reddish tints before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, with only the root system surviving underground until spring regrowth.

funFact: Yellow sundrops are considered excellent 'pollinator magnets' by the Royal Horticultural Society because their daytime blooming schedule and bright yellow color specifically attract bees and butterflies, while most of their evening primrose cousins cater to night-flying moths instead!
confusionNotes: Yellow sundrops can be confused with other yellow four-petaled flowers like wild mustards, but the waxy blue-green leaves and mounding growth habit are distinctive. Remember: if it has yellow cross-shaped flowers but silvery-blue leaves that feel waxy, you've found sundrops!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'evening primrose,' yellow sundrops actually bloom during the day, which can confuse beginners. The evening primrose family got its name from other members that open at dusk, but several species like sundrops break this rule and prefer daylight hours.
compareHints: Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones. Unlike the taller small sundrops, yellow sundrops form more compact, mounding clumps and have larger, showier flowers. The waxy leaf coating is a key feature that separates it from most other Oenothera species in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
